'''''Agrimonia procera''''', the '''fragrant agrimony''',<ref name="jarvis-2020">{{cite book |last1=Jarvis |first1=Peter J. |title=The Pelagic Dictionary of Natural History of the British Isles |date=2020 |publisher=Pelagic |location=Exeter |isbn=9781784271947}}</ref> is a species of [[flowering plant]] belonging to the family [[Rosaceae]].<ref name="POWO">{{cite web |title=Agrimonia procera Wallr. {{!}} Plants of the World Online {{!}} Kew Science |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:720304-1 |website=Plants of the World Online |access-date=10 February 2021 |language=en}}</ref>

It is native to Europe and Southern Africa.<ref name="POWO" />

==Description==
A [[herbaceous plant|herbaceous]] [[perennial plant]] which grows to about 1 m tall, with a branched or unbranched green stem covered in [[trichome#Plant trichomes|glandular]] hairs which are 2 mm long or slightly longer. The leaves are [[pinnate]] with 3-6 pairs of oval, distinctly serrated primary leaflets, an irregular number of secondary leaflets, and a similar or slightly larger terminal leaflet. The underside of the leaves are studded with yellow, shiny glands which produce a sweet aroma. Flowers are arranged in long [[raceme]]s at the top of the stem(s). Each flower has 5 yellow [[petal]]s, 5-20 [[stamen]]s and 2 [[Gynoecium#Carpels|carpels]]. The [[hypanthium]] develops into a characteristic brown, oval or bell-shaped fruit with deep lateral grooves and a double ring of hooked bristles around its centre, which contains 1 or 2 [[achene]]s.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |publisher=C&M Floristics |location=Middlewood Green |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

It is easy to confuse fragrant agrimony with [[Agrimonia eupatoria|common agrimony]], which has a similar distribution and habitat. The key differences are that fragrant agrimony has longer hairs (and no short hairs) on the stem, leaves that are more deeply and acutely serrated and with more glands on the underside, and fruits with shorter grooves and reflexed bristles. These hooked bristles are the most useful feature to use when it is not possible to compare the two species side-by-side: if you imagine they emerge from the fruit's "equator", then most of the bristles point "southwards" or at most straight out in common agrimony, but in fragrant agrimony some distinctly point "northwards" (towards the stalk).<ref name='Stace'/><ref>{{cite web |last1=Rich |first1=T.C.G. |title=Plant Crib: Agrimonia eupatoria/A. procera |url=https://bsbi.org/wp-content/uploads/dlm_uploads/Agrimonia_Crib.pdf}}</ref>

==Ecology==
The habitat of fragrant agrimony in Britain and Ireland is woodland margin, scrub, road verges and tall grassland, on circumneutral (neither acid nor alkaline), sometimes damp, soils. It is confined to the lowlands, being known only up to 335 m at Fortingall, in Perthshire.<ref>{{cite web |last1=BRC |title=Agrimonia procera |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/plantatlas/plant/agrimonia-procera |website=Online Atlas of the British and Irish Flora}}</ref> It is a bigger, bushier and more leafy plant than common agrimony and is far less common, although its overall range is similar. It is most abundant along rides in [[Quercus robur|oak]] or sometimes [[Fraxinus excelsior|ash]] woods, or in field edges nearby.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Lockton |first1=Alex |last2=Whild |first2=Sarah |title=The Flora and Vegetation of Shropshire |date=2015 |publisher=Shropshire Botanical Society |location=Montford Bridge |url=https://archive.org/details/flora-and-vegetation-of-shropshire-2015}}</ref> It flowers rather later than common agrimony, typically from late July in southern England.

Little is known about the interactions between fragrant agrimony and other species. The British database of insects and their food plants<ref>{{cite web |title=Insects and their food plants |url=https://www.brc.ac.uk/dbif/hostsresults.aspx?hostid=202}}</ref> lists only one aphid, ''[[Acyrthosiphon]] malvae'' (Mosley, 1841) that has been observed on this plant. The hooked seeds are ideal for facilitating dispersal by animals, but which are primarily involved is not known.

==Distribution==
The native distribution of fragrant agrimony is thought to include almost all of [[Europe]] and [[South Africa]], but none of the territory between.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew |title=Agrimonia procera Wallr. |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:720304-1 |website=Plants of the World Online}}</ref> This strikingly [[disjunct distribution]] is highly unusual and could be due to transportation of the seeds by migrating wild birds or a more recent introduction by humans. In South Africa, however, it is considered native and is officially categorised as "least concern",<ref>{{cite web |last1=South African National Biodiversity Institute |title=Red List of South African Plants |url=http://redlist.sanbi.org/species.php?species=3453-6 |access-date=7 February 2022}}</ref> although some sources, such as the citizen science website iNaturalist,<ref>{{cite web |title=Scented agrimony |url=https://www.inaturalist.org/guide_taxa/751782 |website=iNaturalist}}</ref> describe it as invasive there.

==Uses==
Fragrant agrimony is palatable to livestock and occurs in grazed woodland, meadows and pastures. Like other species of agrimony, it is reported to have beneficial effects on the health of experimental animals and to reduce inflammation in cells ''in vitro''. Chemicals under investigation include the bitter-tasting compound agrimoniin and various flavonoids.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Graeber |first1=T. |title=Agrimonia procera exerts antimicrobial effects, modulates the expression of defensins and cytokines in colonocytes and increases the immune response in lipopolysaccharide-challenged piglets |journal=BMC Veterinary Research |date=2018 |volume=14 |page=346 |doi=10.1186/s12917-018-1680-0 |url=https://bmcvetres.biomedcentral.com/articles/10.1186/s12917-018-1680-0|doi-access=free |pmc=6238359 }}</ref>
Agrimony is often touted as having health benefits in humans, although medical sources stress that evidence about efficacy and safety is generally lacking.<ref>{{cite web |title=Agrimony - Uses, Side Effects, and More |url=https://www.webmd.com/vitamins/ai/ingredientmono-604/agrimony |website=WebMD |access-date=7 February 2022}}</ref> Claims about its use in the past may be exaggerated: the Roman author [[Aulus Cornelius Celsus|Celsus]], who was influential in medicine for over a thousand years, only mentions agrimony as a possible cure for snake bites.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Celsus |first1=Aurus Cornelius |authorlink=Aulus Cornelius Celsus|title=De Medicina |url= https://penelope.uchicago.edu/Thayer/E/Roman/Texts/Celsus/home.html |access-date=January 4, 2022}}</ref> 

With its bitter taste, agrimony is popular in [[herbal tea]]s. Most advertisements for herbal teas specify common rather than fragrant agrimony, but it is not always clear that people have differentiated between the two.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Slaughton |first1=John |title=9 Surprising Benefits Of Agrimony |url=https://www.organicfacts.net/health-benefits/herbs-and-spices/agrimony.html |website=Organic Facts |access-date=7 February 2022}}</ref>
